bytes.header: Header: version 0, no constant segregation, no size field
bytes.type: SigmaProp type code — the body is a single constant of type SigmaProp

p2pk.title: Anatomy of a P2PK tree: 0008cd…
p2pk.p1: The most common contract on Ergo is “only the owner of this public key can spend” — the ErgoScript equivalent of { pk }. Every ordinary wallet address (starting with 9) represents this tree. It always has the form {{prefix}} + a 33-byte public key:
p2pk.p2:
Just 36 bytes. That is why a
P2PK address
doesn’t store the whole tree, only the 33-byte public key — wallets and nodes always know how to rebuild the tree by prepending 0008cd.

fee.label: Fee contract
fee.note: P2S — collected by the block’s miner; the reward box it goes into is locked for 720 blocks

p2pk.label: P2PK
p2pk.note: sigmaProp(pk) — needs the key holder’s signature

p2sh.label: P2SH
p2sh.note: hash of a script — revealed when spent

kinds.title: Common kinds of guard script
kinds.p1: Written in ErgoScript, compiled to an <ergotree>ErgoTree</ergotree> (byte layout below) and placed in R1:

pk.title: 1. Public key — an ordinary wallet (P2PK)
pk.code: sigmaProp(pk)   // pk is your public key
pk.p:
Only the holder of the matching private key can sign. Every address starting with 9 is this script with a different key — see
Addresses
.

time.title: 2. Time lock
time.p: The key holder still has to sign, but the transaction is only valid once the chain has passed block 1,200,000. Used for vesting and time-limited escrow.

multi.title: 3. Multiple signatures / threshold
multi.code:
atLeast(2, Coll(pk1, pk2, pk3))   // any 2 of 3
pk1 && pk2                          // both must sign
pk1 || pk2                          // either one — a ring signature

outputs.title: 4. Conditions on the outputs — multi-step contracts
outputs.p: Anyone can spend this box, as long as the first output keeps at least the old ERG and carries this same script. Such “self-replicating” boxes are how Ergo builds stateful contracts: the emission contract, oracle pools and DEXes are all variations of this pattern. See the block reward transaction in Transactions.

hash.title: 5. Hash lock (HTLC)
hash.p: The spender must reveal a secret with a given hash (passed in through the context variable getVar). Combined with a time lock, this is the basis of cross-chain atomic swaps.

guards.title: Locks on boxes just created on mainnet
guards.caption: Most boxes are P2PK — ordinary wallets. Every transaction also creates a fee box (P2S). Now and then you'll see a long P2S box: those are DeFi contracts, oracles or token mints.

intro.p1: Every box on Ergo carries a piece of code that decides who (or under what conditions) may spend it. That code is stored on the blockchain as an ErgoTree — a syntax tree serialized into bytes. What developers actually write is ErgoScript, a Scala-like language that compiles down to ErgoTree.
intro.p2: In other words: ErgoScript is for humans, ErgoTree is for nodes. A node never sees ErgoScript — it only reads bytes and evaluates the tree.

script.title: ErgoScript: what does a contract look like?
script.p1: An ErgoScript contract is an expression that returns a SigmaProp — a “statement that must be proven”. A simple example:
script.cond: sigmaProp(HEIGHT > 1000000) — an ordinary boolean condition that the node checks by itself from the context (the current block height).
script.pk: alicePk — a sigma proposition: the spender must produce a cryptographic proof that they know Alice’s secret key.
script.p3: A script can read a lot from the transaction context: SELF (the box being spent), INPUTS, OUTPUTS, CONTEXT.dataInputs, HEIGHT, the registers R4–R9 of any box… This lets a box set rules for the transaction that spends it — for example “the first output must pay at least 100 ERG back to this address”. That is exactly the “extended” in eUTXO.

loops.title: No infinite loops
loops.text: ErgoScript has no unbounded loops or recursion. The execution cost of every script is metered and capped, so a contract can never make a node “hang”. For multi-step logic, you chain several transactions together.

guard.title: Guard scripts: what an ErgoScript contract actually does
guard.p1: An ErgoScript program placed in a box's register R1 is called a guard script: it decides who may spend the box and under what conditions. On Ergo there is nothing but boxes and guard scripts, so before looking at bytes, here is what a guard script is for.

validator.title: A guard script is a validator, not a program
validator.p1: On Ethereum a contract is a program with its own state, and you “call its functions”. On Ergo a guard script does not run when you send money to a box — it runs exactly once, when someone tries to spend the box. At that moment the node executes the script against the full context of the transaction being checked:
validator.self: The box being spent — its value, tokens and registers.
validator.io: Every box going into and out of the transaction. A script can demand that outputs have a particular shape.
validator.height: The current block height — used for time locks.
validator.miner: The key of the miner of this block — the fee contract uses it.
validator.p2: The script must return true for the box to be spent; if it returns false, the whole transaction is rejected and nothing changes. That is why the Ergo and Cardano communities call guard scripts validators: they only approve or reject a transaction you have already built — they never do anything on their own.

sigma.title: True/false … plus a signature
sigma.p1: More precisely, a guard script doesn't return a bare true/false bit but a sigma proposition (SigmaProp). The node reduces the script against the context: ordinary conditions (height, output values…) are evaluated to true/false right away, while the “prove you know the secret key” parts are kept as a tree of cryptographic conditions. Whoever spends the box must supply a signature satisfying that tree — that signature is the spending proof attached to the input. The whole mechanism is explained in sigma protocols.

ok.title: The box is spent when
ok.c1: every ordinary condition in the script holds, and
ok.c2: the signature (proof) satisfies the remaining cryptographic part, and
ok.c3: the script's execution cost is within the limit.

bad.title: The transaction is rejected when
bad.c1: any input's script evaluates to false,
bad.c2: a signature for an input is missing or wrong,
bad.c3: or the script reduces to an absolute false (the box is “burned” forever — nobody can spend it).

address.title: The script determines the address
address.p1: An Ergo address is just a readable encoding of the ErgoTree, so two boxes with identical guard scripts have the same address. That is why every fee box on the network sits at a single P2S address (starting with 2iHkR7…), and why a “contract's balance” is simply the sum of the boxes carrying that script. You can split any address back into its script with the address decoder.

layout.title: The byte layout of an ErgoTree
layout.p1: This section is for readers who want to read a tree byte by byte, as the address decoder does. If you only care about what contracts do, skip to the fee-contract example below. A serialized ErgoTree consists of four parts, in this order:
layout.header: Header (1 byte): the low 3 bits are the version; bit 0x08 signals that a size field follows; bit 0x10 signals that the tree uses constant segregation.
layout.size: Size (optional) — the length of the rest of the tree, written as a VLQ (a compact variable-length integer). Mandatory from ErgoTree version 1 onwards, so a node can skip a tree without fully understanding it.
layout.consts: Constants list (with constant segregation): a count, then each constant as type ‖ value.
layout.body: Tree body: the expression itself, written as opcodes followed by their operands — each operation comes first, then the things it operates on (pre-order traversal).

h00.text: The most compact form. Constants sit inline in the tree body. Most P2PK wallet addresses use this header.

h10.text: Constants are pulled out to the front of the tree; the body only holds “placeholders” (ConstantPlaceholder, opcode 0x73).

h18.text: Adds bit 0x08 (the size flag). Version 1 and above always include the size.

seg.title: Constant segregation: separating constants from logic
seg.p1: Imagine a thousand people using the same time-lock contract, differing only in their public key and unlock height. If constants were mixed into the tree, every box would be a completely different byte string. With constant segregation, all constants are lifted to the front of the tree, and the body only contains references 7300, 7301… (placeholder 0, placeholder 1…). The benefits:
seg.template: Template recognition: two boxes using the same contract share the same body even if their constants differ. Explorers and dApps can recognize the contract type just by comparing tree bodies.
seg.cache: Caching: a node can parse and cost-estimate the body once and reuse it.
seg.subst: Constant substitution: a script can use substConstants to build a new tree from a template by swapping a constant — the fee contract below uses exactly this trick.

fee.title: A real example: the miner fee contract
fee.p1: On Ergo, the transaction fee is not “the leftover difference” as in Bitcoin. The sender creates an explicit fee output, locked by a fixed ErgoTree that every wallet uses. Here is that tree (105 bytes):

bytes.c2: Constant #2: a 54-byte Coll[Byte] — itself an ErgoTree (the “miner reward” template)
bytes.c3: Constant #3: Coll[Int](1) — the index substConstants replaces; constant #4: Int 1 — for the OUTPUTS.size == 1 check
bytes.body: Tree body: opcodes referring to constants via 73xx

fee.p2: Rewritten in ErgoScript, its meaning is roughly:
fee.p3: Nobody needs to sign to spend a fee box. Anyone can “spend” it — but the contract forces the coins into a box locked to minerPubKey (the key of the current block’s miner, taken from the header), and that box only unlocks after 720 blocks (~1 day). In practice, miners add the fee-collecting transaction to their own block.

g.title: Why the key of point G?
g.text: Inside the 54-byte template there is a public key starting with 0279be667e… — that is the generator point G of the secp256k1 curve, used as a “placeholder” value that substConstants replaces with the miner’s key. You’ll meet point G again in the w field of an Autolykos v2 solution.

cost.title: Execution cost
cost.p1: Every operation in an ErgoTree has a cost. When validating a transaction, a node adds up the cost of all input scripts; if it exceeds the block limit (a parameter miners can vote to change), the transaction is rejected. This is how Ergo allows powerful contracts without Ethereum-style “gas”: there are no unbounded loops, so cost is always bounded, and the node stops a script as soon as its accumulated cost exceeds the limit (since v5.0, cost is counted during execution rather than estimated up front).
